kakekotoba.interaction: Primarily literal 'night' here; while よ can pivot to 世 (world/life) elsewhere in the canon, in this poem the grammar and context (夏の夜は = 'the summer night') keep it firmly denoting the night itself with no secondary 世 reading grammatically activated, so this is noted but not counted as a true kakekotoba.

bipartite.kami_theme: The short summer night has already ended while it still felt like early evening (yoi) — a statement of temporal astonishment at how briefly night lasted.
bipartite.shimo_theme: The speaker wonders in which part of the clouds the moon could possibly be lodging/resting now, since dawn came too fast for it to have completed its journey across the sky.
bipartite.pivot_note: The kami-no-ku establishes the physical/temporal fact (the brevity of the summer night, dawn arriving while it still feels like early evening), and the shimo-no-ku is the speaker's playful inferential leap: since the moon had no time to set in the west, it must still be hiding somewhere among the clouds. The whole poem turns on a witty causal deduction from an observed natural fact (short night) to a whimsical unseen event (the moon's whereabouts).

kigo.note: The short summer night (natsu no yo) is itself the poem's explicit and central seasonal marker — classical poetics prized the phenomenon of nights so short in summer that dusk seems to touch dawn directly, a marvel distinct from the long nights of autumn/winter praised elsewhere in the canon. The moon (月), though often an autumn kigo in isolation, is here subordinated to and reframed by the summer-night conceit, so summer governs the poem rather than the moon carrying its usual autumnal association.

source_jp:
夏の夜は
まだ宵ながら
明けぬるを
雲のいづくに
月やどるらむ
